description: We are just having fun, not too competitive
summary: LunaPoint is a free, tool that tells you whether a spot on the Moon, at a chosen touchdown time, will have sunlight for power, a direct radio link to Earth and ground flat enough to land on. It computes where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky from the site and tests them against the real terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data, then gives a go or no-go using the Artemis landing limits. A comparison table shows what a launch slip does to the same spot week by week. A 3D lander then flies the whole trip, from Earth to touchdown, on that terrain. This matters most at the lunar south pole, where the Sun skims the horizon and a shift of a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a mission has power and can call home.
details:
LunaPoint answers one question for any spot on the Moon at any touchdown time: will a lander there have sunlight for power, a direct radio link to Earth, and ground flat enough to land on?

How it works: a lunar ephemeris (checked against NASA JPL Horizons) gives the Sun’s and Earth’s positions in the sky from the site. These are tested against the true terrain horizon, which is ray-traced through NASA LRO LOLA elevation data. Slopes over 100 m come from the same data. The app then gives a GO / NO-GO verdict using Artemis landing limits (slope under 10°). A comparison table shows what a launch slip does to the same spot, week by week. A 3D lander flies the whole mission, from Earth through lunar orbit, braking, approach and touchdown, onto the real terrain at the chosen spot. Ground cameras film the landing, and the lander tips over if the slope is too steep.

Go/No Go

  • ten graded checks: landing-ellipse safety, Sun angle for hazard cameras, comms during powered descent, a 14-day battery and thermal simulation, and longest night against battery endurance
  • link budget and signal delay
  • a mission timeline back to launch
  • an example fuel budget
  • the best dates in the next 120 days
  • a CSV report

Why it matters: at the south pole the Sun skims the horizon. Moving a few hundred metres, or a few days, can decide whether a mission has power and can come home.

Built with: TypeScript, React, three.js, Bun. It runs entirely in the browser with no server, and works on phones.
